# Architecture Data, Knowledge, and Representation {#sec-data-representations-world-models}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"The limits of my language mean the limits of my world."*
>
> — Ludwig Wittgenstein, *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus* (1922) [@Wittgenstein1922Tractatus]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** Ludwig Wittgenstein tied the limits of language to the limits
of one's world. The architecture claim is narrower. A method can change only
the design state exposed to it. If a representation has no way to express a
coherence assumption, software dependency, or physical limit, the method
cannot preserve it deliberately.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
What must an AI-assisted architecture system preserve when its data comes from
changing designs, costly tools, workloads, and sources that do not always
agree?
:::

An image-classification dataset can present each item as an array of pixels and
a label. An architecture result cannot be reduced to a number and a name. A
cycle count, timing report, or power estimate applies to a particular design,
software image, workload, tool path, version, and set of conditions. One wrong
connection or protocol assumption can invalidate the design even when its text
looks similar to many valid examples.

Architecture data also arrives in forms that were created for different jobs.
Specifications state requirements. Source code and register-transfer-level
(RTL) designs define executable or buildable artifacts. Traces record selected
workload behavior. Simulators, formal tools, synthesis flows, physical-design
tools, prototypes, and silicon return different measurements and check results.
Review comments and rejected alternatives preserve decisions that no tool
report contains. These sources differ in access, freshness, cost, coverage, and
what they can establish.

A *representation* is the form in which selected properties of a source or
design are made available to a method. A native RTL file, a typed graph, a table
of measurements, a retrieval index, and a learned embedding can all represent
part of an architecture problem. None preserves everything. The choice
determines which relationships remain visible, which designs can be expressed,
and which mistakes a later method may fail to notice.

Architects often use *representation* to mean a semantic design abstraction or
level together with its legal objects and transformations. In machine learning,
the same word often means an encoding or learned feature space fit for a task
[@BengioEtAl2013RepresentationLearning]. Their shared test is which semantics
and distinctions survive for the intended operation and check. An AI-assisted
architecture system often needs both exact design semantics for tools and
checks and feature spaces for learned methods. RTL, an intermediate
representation, a constraint set, a graph, and an embedding therefore preserve
different properties and serve different purposes. They are not
interchangeable.

Raw sources become useful data only after the project identifies them, aligns
their versions and units, records the conditions under which they were
obtained, and checks that their labels or tool returns mean what the dataset
claims. Some of that data becomes durable project knowledge. Other parts remain
live project state that must change with the checked-in design, software,
workload, constraints, and unresolved issues. An architecture foundation model
may supply broad prior knowledge about mechanisms and common designs. Its
weights do not contain the authoritative truth about the current project.

Without those distinctions, a method can retrieve stale guidance, compare
unlike tool returns, or optimize an encoding that omitted a controlling
relationship. The project must therefore link native artifacts, checked data,
durable project knowledge, live state, and derived representations. Architects
must be able to inspect those links before they choose a method, connect a
tool, or interpret a result.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Identify essential conditions that separate architecture data from generic examples.
- Map workloads, tool results, and acquisition costs to executable design states.
- Build datasets that explicitly handle tool failures, hard boundaries, and missing outcomes.
- Separate durable knowledge from live project state to trace facts to authoritative sources.
- Select representations that preserve identity, design legality, constraints, and check results.
:::

## Why Architecture Data Is Different

Architecture data is heterogeneous, conditional, expensive to acquire, and
often proprietary. A specification paragraph, an RTL module, a performance
counter trace, and a routed timing report are not interchangeable samples. Each
preserves different relationships and omits different conditions. Their
differences are part of the data rather than noise to remove.

Rows also share dependencies. Two results may come from the same design
ancestor, generated artifact, workload trace, software image, tool model, or
earlier decision. A failed physical-design run may return no complete metric,
while a timing check may establish only that a threshold was crossed. Counting
these records as independent examples with fixed labels would hide both their
lineage and their missingness.

Architecture correctness adds a harder boundary. A plausible token sequence can
still connect the wrong signals, violate a protocol, drop a reset condition, or
refer to a stale hierarchy. More superficially similar examples do not repair
the omitted relationship. A usable representation must therefore preserve the
structure and conditions that let a tool or reviewer detect the mistake.

The sources may remain in separate project systems. A configuration schema,
workload manifest, repository revision, run directory, and review record do not
need to become one database. They do need shared identities that let another
architect determine which artifacts and measurements describe the same design
and conditions.

Carrying those relationships into later work requires several transformations
(@fig-architecture-data-progression). Heterogeneous sources first become a
checked dataset. Some checked information becomes durable knowledge, while
current hardware, software, workload, and constraint facts
remain live project state. Native artifacts, explicit structures, and optional
learned views then expose different properties to a method without becoming
interchangeable.

![**Architecture sources become method-ready without surrendering their source
of record.** Heterogeneous source artifacts are checked into a dataset, then
separated into durable knowledge and current project state before they support
linked native, structured, and optional learned representations. Source
identity, versions, acquisition conditions, and access limits remain attached
through the handoff, so a derived view can add a capability without replacing
the authoritative artifact.](images/F4-architecture-data-progression){#fig-architecture-data-progression
width="98%" fig-alt="A left-to-right sequence begins with heterogeneous
architecture sources, passes through a checked dataset, separates durable
knowledge from current project state, and forms linked native, structured, and
optional learned representations before method choice. A bar across the bottom
states that source identity, versions, acquisition conditions, and links remain
attached throughout. Native artifacts remain the source of record."}

A checked observation records what a source returned under specific
conditions. Only the responsible project source determines which fact applies
now. Neither role can be assigned to an artifact whose source is unknown, so
the work starts by identifying those sources and what each one can answer.

## Sources of Architecture Data

Papers, specifications, source code, RTL, traces, tool reports, failed
candidates, review notes, and field observations preserve different
relationships. The relevant distinction is not text versus numbers, but rather
which question a source can answer, which context it omits, and how a reader
can connect it to the current design (@tbl-dataset-capability).

| **Source structure** | **What it can preserve** | **What it cannot establish alone** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paper, manual, or specification | Concepts, requirements, interfaces, prior findings, and source-linked rationale. | The current project version or whether a local implementation satisfies the requirement. |
| Question and answer or design note | Focused reasoning, calculations, and review rationale. | Executable state, complete dependencies, or conditions not written into the note. |
| Code, RTL, configuration, or typed intermediate representation | Concrete structure, parameter values, interfaces, and buildable state within the properties the format expresses. | Workload coverage, design intent, or physical effects that require later tools. |
| Workload trace or profile | Observed software behavior under a stated capture or sampling policy. | Behavior outside the captured population or effects the collection method cannot observe. |
| Tool run and report | A result under a particular design, tool, configuration, seed, model, and workload. | A general rule beyond those conditions. |
| Rejected candidate or review decision | A boundary that mattered, the conditions that exposed it, and the reason work stopped. | Whether the same rejection still applies after the design or conditions change. |

: **Source structure determines what can be carried into later work.** More
data does not repair a missing relationship, version, or condition.
{#tbl-dataset-capability tbl-colwidths="[24,36,30]"}

Each source preserves some relationships and leaves other claims unsupported.
More source volume cannot make one structure authoritative for fields it does
not own.

For a cache or accelerator study, source discovery should follow the
architecture path that the decision crosses. Workload and application sources
carry binaries, inputs, phases, profiles, traces, and service behavior.
Compiler and runtime sources show the transformations, schedules, libraries,
and software settings applied to that workload. ISA, microarchitecture, cache,
memory-controller, and interconnect artifacts expose interfaces, parameters,
counters, and model state. RTL, assertions, formal results, and coverage
databases show implemented logic together with the properties and stimuli
checked. Synthesis, timing, power, place-and-route, and reliability flows add
implementation- and condition-specific results. Emulation, FPGA prototypes,
post-silicon tests, and field telemetry extend coverage into long-running and
deployed behavior. The property and transfer claim determine which of these
sources belong, so a dataset need not collect every artifact in the stack.

Expert judgment is also conditioned data. Reusable judgment records the
evidence shown to the expert, the criteria applied, the expertise and role
relevant to the question, the expert's confidence, and any disagreement or
limiting context. A schedule-driven choice, local convention, or estimate
remains labeled as such rather than becoming an architecture fact. Whether that
judgment supports a later claim belongs to @sec-feedback-verification-trust.

These sources establish what information may exist. Access, permission to use
it, and the claims that another group can check are separate constraints.

## Public, Private, and Licensed Architecture Data

The responsible source may also be private, licensed, or access-restricted.
That boundary does not make a convenient public substitute authoritative. The
representation should retain the source identity, version, responsible owner,
access limit, and conditions under which it applies, with a link that an
authorized reviewer can resolve.

Artifact-level license and permitted-use fields distinguish access from
permission to use a source for training or retrieval, transform it,
redistribute it, or publish derivatives. A project should preserve the source's
permissions, restrictions, and provenance with derived datasets, retrieval
indexes, learned representations, and model weights. A large-scale audit of AI
datasets found frequent license omissions and misclassifications, which makes
retaining source, attribution, and license metadata part of dataset
construction rather than release-time cleanup [@LongpreEtAl2024DataProvenance].
The audit does not determine what a license permits for a particular
architecture project. Whether a restriction applies to a derived artifact
depends on the source, intended use, and governing law. The project should seek
legal review when that applicability is uncertain rather than assuming that
transformation removed the restriction or automatically carried it into every
derivative.

Generated-output provenance and project confidentiality add two different
questions. The project should retain the retrieved passages, supplied context,
model and endpoint identity, and any similarity or overlap checks used to
examine generated RTL, scripts, or constraints. These records expose known
inputs and can flag reproduction or close similarity. They do not reveal every
pretraining source or establish permission, noninfringement, or clearance to
publish. Separately, a source may be authorized for internal use while a
specification, netlist fragment, timing constraint, or tool report still may not
leave the approved computing boundary. The project therefore needs explicit
access, egress, and retention rules for model endpoints, retrieval indexes,
logs, and caches.

Outside-review access is separate again. It asks what evidence another group
can inspect, not whether the project may use or transmit a private source.
When raw sources cannot be released, reproducibility can still be designed into
the public claim. A team can publish data schemas, collection and cleaning
procedures, workload definitions, artifact hashes, aggregate statistics, tool
and version identities, executable harnesses, and the held-out policy while
keeping restricted artifacts under their declared access controls. A public
subset can exercise the same schema and harness, expose parsing and derivation
paths, and let an independent group test which aggregate or comparative results
reproduce. The release must state which claims can be checked from public
material and which still depend on private evidence. A reproducible procedure
is not a public replication of an unavailable measurement.

*Datasheets for Datasets* provides a standard way to document why a dataset was
created, what it contains, how it was collected, how it may be used, and how it
will be maintained [@GebruEtAl2021Datasheets]. Architecture datasets need that
baseline plus the identities that determine what a sample means. These include
the artifact and tool versions, workload and physical conditions, failed or
censored runs, access and license terms, and the exact claims that another team
can reproduce. A dataset card can explain the collection without making every
sample applicable to a new design.

Documentation states what a collection claims to contain and how it was
assembled. Acquisition context establishes which source population, filters,
tools, and measurement conditions actually produced its records.

Field and fleet observations need further acquisition context. Record the
deployed hardware and software versions, workload population, sampling policy,
measurement conditions, privacy or redaction rules, and collection cost with
the observation. A result from deployed systems describes that version and
population. It does not automatically become a training label or a conclusion
about the next design.

Public availability is only the first filter. The OpenRTLSet collection started
with approximately 103,000 permissively licensed public C/C++ repositories.
The authors' synthesizability screen retained approximately 12,000, and their
Vitis HLS flow successfully generated Verilog from approximately 1,000
repositories [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. The attrition across these three
repository-level stages, rather than the initial amount of public code,
determines what can enter this corpus (@fig-public-code-to-rtl). The resulting
24,000 Verilog modules use a different unit because one successful repository
can produce many modules, so module count is an annotation rather than a fourth
attrition stage.

```{python}
#| label: fig-public-code-to-rtl
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Public code becomes architecture data only after several filters.** In the OpenRTLSet C/C++ collection path, approximately 103,000 permissively licensed repositories became approximately 12,000 repositories after the authors' synthesizability screen, and approximately 1,000 successfully produced Verilog through their Vitis HLS flow [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. The reported 24,000 output modules use a different unit and therefore appear as an annotation rather than another point. These pipeline-specific counts are not universal GitHub or HLS success rates.
#| out-width: "88%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale connected-dot plot with three stages from the OpenRTLSet C and C++ collection pipeline. Approximately 103,000 permissively licensed repositories enter the pipeline, 12,000 remain after the authors' synthesizability screen, and 1,000 successfully generate Verilog through Vitis HLS. A separate note states that the successful repositories produced approximately 24,000 Verilog modules, which is a different unit."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Values are approximate counts transcribed from Sections III-A1 and III-A2 of
# OpenRTLSet [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. Receipt:
# data/source-receipts/chapter4-openrtlset-funnel.csv. Accessed 2026-07-30.
stages = [
    "Permissively licensed\nC/C++ repositories",
    "After authors'\nsynthesizability screen",
    "Successful Vitis HLS\nto Verilog",
]
counts = [103_000, 12_000, 1_000]
display_counts = ["≈103,000", "≈12,000", "≈1,000"]
y = [2, 1, 0]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.7, 2.55))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.38, right=0.92, top=0.88, bottom=0.30)

ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(500, 220_000)
ax.plot(counts, y, color=COLORS["muted"], linewidth=1.2, zorder=1)
ax.scatter(
    counts,
    y,
    s=46,
    color=COLORS["workload"],
    edgecolor="white",
    linewidth=0.8,
    zorder=2,
)

for x_value, y_value, label in zip(counts, y, display_counts):
    ax.text(
        x_value * 1.14,
        y_value,
        label,
        ha="left",
        va="center",
        fontsize=6.4,
        fontweight="bold",
        color=COLORS["workload_ink"],
    )

ax.set_yticks(y)
ax.set_yticklabels(stages, fontsize=6.2)
ax.set_xlabel("approximate repositories remaining (log scale)", fontsize=6.2)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.0, length=2.5, width=0.6)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0, pad=5)
ax.grid(axis="x", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6)
ax.text(
    0.0,
    -0.36,
    "Output annotation: ≈24,000 Verilog modules from ≈1,000 successful repositories",
    transform=ax.transAxes,
    ha="left",
    va="top",
    fontsize=5.8,
    color=COLORS["muted"],
)

for spine in ["top", "right", "left"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

About 11.7 percent of the starting repositories
survived the authors' initial screen, and about 1 percent successfully produced
Verilog through this particular pipeline. Those derived ratios describe the
authors' repository search, license policy, screen, and tool flow, rather than
estimating how much public C/C++ is synthesizable in general. The example makes a
narrower point: collecting public source, deciding what is legally usable,
screening it, executing a conversion tool, and accounting for failures are
distinct dataset-construction steps.

Public architecture datasets also differ in their unit of observation and in
the question they can answer (@tbl-public-architecture-data). Their counts are
not comparable, and these four examples do not establish global coverage of
architecture data. A Verilog module, a repository-context completion, a
physical-design run, and a question-answer pair each expose a different part of
the design problem.

| **Collection and observation unit** | **Supported task** | **Key missing context** | **Failed or rejected data status** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OpenRTLSet observes one extracted Verilog module from public Verilog, translated VHDL, or C/C++ passed through HLS [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. | Fine-tuning and evaluating module-level Verilog generation. | Full project state, workload and software conditions, physical measurements, per-module functional checks, and a repository-disjoint split are not established. | Failed VHDL and Vitis HLS conversions are excluded. The source does not report a released corpus of failed artifacts and structured rejection reasons. |
| RTL-Repo observes one target-line completion with the surrounding Verilog repository as context [@AllamShalan2024RTLRepo]. | Long-context, multi-file Verilog autocompletion measured with exact match and edit similarity. | Functional, synthesis, simulation, workload, power, performance, area, and physical-design evidence. The reported train and test counts do not establish a repository-disjoint split. | No design tool is executed for the observation. Repositories rejected by the collection filters are not reported as retained records. |
| CircuitNet observes one back-end design run and retained layout under a declared synthesis and physical-design setting [@ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet]. | Cross-stage congestion, design rule check violation, and IR-drop prediction from graph and image-like features. | Front-end software and workload behavior, live project history, and a canonical grouping rule for evaluation. | The authors attempted 12,960 runs and retained 10,242 layouts after excluding failed runs. Failure artifacts and causes are not reported as retained. |
| QuArch v0.1 observes one expert-validated multiple-choice question-answer pair about a computer architecture topic [@PrakashEtAl2025QuArch]. | Evaluating architecture knowledge retrieval and fine-tuning language models for that task. | Executable design state, workload and software identity, tool returns, physical measurements, and signoff evidence. | Validation removes questions without definitive answers or with scope too narrow for the benchmark. Rejected questions and reasons are not reported as retained. |

: **A dataset supports only the task and context carried by its observations.**
Module code, repository context, executed layouts, and architecture questions
are useful for different purposes and leave different parts of a design
decision unobserved.
{#tbl-public-architecture-data tbl-colwidths="[27,22,29,26]"}

Missing context is not the same as poor data quality. QuArch can be a
well-validated test of architecture knowledge without describing a live design
project. CircuitNet can provide executed physical-design observations without
recording the behavior of the software that might eventually run on the chip.
The architect must match the collection to the property and transfer claim
rather than treat public availability or sample count as sufficient evidence.

Public sources make comparison and reuse possible, but they usually omit
proprietary design context. Community datasets can preserve declared
repositories, flows, and collection choices, yet their quality depends on what
contributors record and release. Internal sources may carry the current design,
review history, and vendor material that a real decision needs, but privacy,
intellectual-property, license, and access limits constrain how they are used.
The dataset must preserve that access status rather than silently replacing a
restricted source with a convenient public one.

ChipNeMo provides one task-specific example. It adapted language models and a
retrieval model using proprietary chip-design material, then evaluated an
engineering assistant, EDA script generation, and bug summarization inside that
setting [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo]. The example shows that internal data can improve
selected internal tasks. It does not establish broad architecture-design
capability, and its proprietary evaluation cannot substitute for an
independently testable claim.

One source remains central to almost every architecture result. The workload
determines which parts of the hardware and software become active.

## Workload State Determines What a Sample Means {#sec-workload-phase-behavior}

Static hardware does not identify what it will run. A workload record must
carry the software image, inputs, scale, trace or profile, phase definitions,
sampling policy, runtime settings, and coverage limits relevant to the study.
Those fields are not background metadata. They determine which hardware
behavior becomes visible.

For the prospective Lighthouse cache study, workload state would include a
versioned snapshot of the bursty, phase-dependent XR workload and the exact
software image used to run it. These declared sources are not retained
artifacts or evidence from an executed study. A trace can expose
frame boundaries, memory behavior, and periods of activity. It may still omit
timing feedback that would have changed the instruction stream, thread
interleaving, or system behavior. A trace captured under one software image
cannot silently stand in for another. The representation must connect
the workload snapshot to the software image, stable frame identifiers, the
collection policy, and the hardware conditions under which it is used.

Representative sampling can reduce detailed simulation cost without changing
the simulator itself. SimPoint clusters recurring execution phases and
simulates representative intervals, while SMARTS uses statistical sampling and
reports confidence for the estimate
[@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint; @WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. The durable
representation point is not which sampling scheme to choose. It is that the
selected intervals, weights, and coverage become part of workload state. A
sampled result without those fields cannot be interpreted or reproduced.

Representativeness is specific to the claim. A workload that exercises a cache
capacity decision may not exercise an accelerator interface, an operating
system transition, or the thermal behavior of a deployed workload mix. Every
measurement must therefore remain linked to the exact workload artifact and
design state that produced it. Once those conditions are explicit, the project
can ask what one such sample costs and what part of the design space it covers.

## Cost and Coverage of a Sample

An architect can examine the same design with an analytical model, trace
replay, cycle-level simulator, RTL simulation, formal analysis, FPGA platform,
or fabricated silicon.
These sources differ in cost, speed, abstraction, and observability
(@fig-observation-source-choice, @tbl-observation-source-limits). They do not form one
fidelity ranking for every property. Post-layout timing analysis may preserve target
timing detail that an FPGA mapping does not, while an FPGA platform may execute
far more workload than that analysis can cover. Silicon can reveal behavior of
the fabricated design but cannot recover a counterfactual configuration that
was never built.

![**Choose observation sources for the property and decision.** Representative analytical,
trace-driven, cycle-level, RTL and gate-level simulation, FPGA or emulation,
and silicon sources offer different coverage, costs, conditions, and blind spots. A study
may combine them, and each recorded observation retains that
context.](images/F4-data-pyramid){#fig-observation-source-choice
fig-alt="A study starts with the architecture property it must observe, then
compares six representative observation sources shown without a universal ranking:
analytical models, trace-driven models, cycle-level simulation, RTL and
gate-level simulation, FPGA or emulation, and fabricated silicon. Each obtained
observation retains its source and version, property coverage, acquisition
cost, conditions, and blind spots." width="100%"}

The study starts with the property it must observe, then compares candidate
sources by coverage, cost, conditions, and blind spots. It may choose several.
The six sources appear in parallel because none is uniformly more informative
than the others. When a source produces an observation, its record keeps the
context needed to interpret and compare it. The choice follows the property and
decision rather than a generic fidelity rank.

The overview groups major observation paths rather than exhaustively listing every distinct return
type. An observation becomes usable only when its intended use is paired with
the limit and provenance its representation must retain
(@tbl-observation-source-limits). Simulation, formal analysis, and
implementation-facing flows remain separate because they return fundamentally different
kinds of results.

| **Source** | **Useful for** | **Important limit to represent** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical model | Fast sensitivity studies and early bounds. | Simplifying equations, calibration range, and omitted interactions. |
| Trace-driven model | Repeatable study of behavior contained in a captured instruction or event stream. | No behavior that depends on timing feedback absent from the trace. |
| Cycle-level simulator | Detailed modeled microarchitectural behavior. | Simulator abstractions, unsupported states, calibration, and execution cost. |
| RTL and gate-level simulation | Logic, interface, and microarchitectural behavior over the exercised testbench and observed properties, including netlist behavior when timing is modeled. | Stimulus and testbench identity, functional and code coverage, unknown-value handling, simulator version, delay annotation, and timing abstractions. |
| Formal analysis | Proof, counterexample, bounded-only, or inconclusive status for a stated property, model, and assumptions. | Exact property and assumptions, abstraction, proof method, bound or completeness argument, vacuity checks, and returned status. |
| Synthesis and static timing or power analysis | Logic transformation and timing, area, or power estimates within the executed netlist and constraint flow. | Libraries, modes, corners, constraints, tool versions, physical approximations, and effects outside the analyzed stage. |
| Place-and-route and physical verification | Placement, routing, extraction, timing, power-integrity, and physical-rule results for the implemented database. | Floorplan and routing state, extraction and signoff models, modes, corners, waivers, tool versions, and unmodeled manufacturing or operating conditions. |
| FPGA or emulation platform | High-throughput functional or timing-model execution after mapping. | Mapping differences, compile cost, debug visibility, and non-transferable ASIC power or timing. |
| Fabricated silicon | Behavior of a physical implementation under measured conditions. | Limited design variants, observability, stepping, test conditions, and inability to answer every counterfactual question. |

: **Every observation source has a useful scope and a blind spot.** The
representation records both so that later chapters can choose and evaluate a
tool path for the actual question.
{#tbl-observation-source-limits tbl-colwidths="[20,34,36]"}

The rows do not order the sources. The property under study determines which
limits are acceptable and whether several sources are needed.

These costs also shape the available data. Expensive observation paths usually
produce fewer observations, and only observations with compatible designs,
workloads, tools, and conditions can support a direct comparison. A large
collection of incompatible reports does not become a dense dataset for the
current study.

A small calculation shows how quickly coverage multiplies acquisition cost.
The calculation uses illustrative assumptions rather than a universal
simulator model. Assume a 1\ GHz target, a 1\ s measured interval, 0.2\ s of
target-time warmup per run, a cycle-level simulator rate of 100,000 target
cycles per wall-clock second, three repetitions, four workloads, and no queue
or setup overhead.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import csv
from pathlib import Path

import _python.plots as _ap

# Receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter4-simulation-time-explosion.csv
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(
    _root / "data" / "source-receipts" / "chapter4-simulation-time-explosion.csv",
    encoding="utf-8",
) as fh:
    _simulation_cost_rows = list(csv.DictReader(fh))

_one_second_row = next(
    row
    for row in _simulation_cost_rows
    if row["target_workload_duration"] == "1 s"
)
measurement_cycles = int(_one_second_row["target_cycles_at_1ghz"])
warmup_cycles = measurement_cycles // 5
simulator_rate = 100_000
repetitions = 3
workloads = 4
single_measurement_hours = measurement_cycles / simulator_rate / 3_600
total_target_cycles = (
    (warmup_cycles + measurement_cycles) * repetitions * workloads
)
total_serial_hours = total_target_cycles / simulator_rate / 3_600
assert _one_second_row["wall_time_at_100kcycle_s"] == "2.8 h"
```

For one measured interval, the target executes
`{python} f"{measurement_cycles:,}"` cycles. At the assumed simulator
rate, those cycles alone require about
`{python} f"{single_measurement_hours:.1f}"` hours. The full serial cost is

$$
T_{\text{serial}} =
\frac{(C_{\text{warmup}} + C_{\text{measure}}) \times R \times W}
{v_{\text{sim}}}.
$$

With the illustrative assumptions, the suite executes
`{python} f"{total_target_cycles / 1e9:.1f}"` billion target cycles and requires
`{python} f"{total_serial_hours:.0f}"` serial simulator hours. A different target
clock, simulator, warmup policy, repetition count, or workload set changes the
result. Target cycles and simulator rate determine time per attempt, while
warmup, repetitions, and workload coverage multiply the cost of obtaining the
conditioned results.

BOOM-Explorer makes the acquisition cost concrete. Each high-fidelity
VLSI-flow evaluation for its dataset of 994 legal microarchitectures took about
six hours at the low end and more than fourteen hours at the high end
[@BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer].

The project must store an acquisition record with each result. That record
identifies the kind and fidelity of the tool run, whether the run completed,
failed, timed out, or was retried, and the repeated seeds or configurations
that produced the result. When available, it also retains uncertainty or an
interval reported by the source, execution and queue time, compute and memory
use, tool or license use, and the human work required for setup, diagnosis,
review, and repair. Ten analytical-model calls,
ten cycle-level simulations, and ten physical-design runs may each create ten
rows, but they do not represent the same cost, coverage, or opportunity to
observe failure. When an exact monetary cost is unavailable, the representation
should preserve the separate resource counts rather than omit them or collapse
them into one number.

Those resource counts belong in the representation even though later work will
use them to choose methods, manage tools, interpret measurements, and compare
complete systems. A stored result must name enough of its source conditions and
acquisition cost for an architect to decide whether it applies and what it took
to produce.

An architecture dataset row must preserve more than a value and label. It ties
the result to a design history, property checks, acquisition status, and the
resources required to obtain it (@tbl-architecture-observations-not-labels).

| **Dataset simplification** | **Architecture sample** | **Consequence for later use** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cheap acquisition** | A result may require scarce licenses, long tool runs, fabrication, setup, diagnosis, and expert review. | Record the resources and human work needed to obtain or fail to obtain it. |
| **Fixed ground-truth label** | A simulator, verifier, or physical tool returns a result for a named property at a stated fidelity and under recorded conditions. | Preserve the property, check, fidelity, and conditions for later interpretation. |
| **Independent, interchangeable rows** | Results may share a design ancestor, generated artifact, workload trace, software image, model, seed, or earlier decision. | Preserve lineage and do not count dependent results as independent support. |
| **Missing data without structure** | Failed, timed-out, and rejected runs are selectively lost, while some violations reveal only that a threshold was crossed. | Retain run status, failure reason, and censored bounds instead of learning only from survivors. |
| **Same fields imply comparability** | Two rows support a direct comparison only when their candidate identities and permitted differences are explicit and the workload, software, tool path, and relevant conditions match. | Keep results with uncontrolled differences as advisory context rather than treating them as samples from the same comparison. |

: **Architecture samples are costly, conditioned results.** Their meaning and
comparability depend on lineage, property checks, acquisition status, and
matched study conditions.
{#tbl-architecture-observations-not-labels tbl-colwidths="[23,42,35]"}

These distinctions change what a stored dataset row contains. A timing row does
not attach a universal correct or incorrect label to a cache. It preserves the
status returned by a named timing check together with the library, constraints,
corner, and tool state. A failed or absent result preserves its run status and
failure reason rather than silently becoming a poor design. An architect must
then determine whether the return marks a feasibility boundary, an
infrastructure failure, or no usable measurement. The failed-run records in
@tbl-negative-traces keep those possibilities separate. These sample semantics
determine how the dataset must be constructed and checked.

## Building and Checking a Usable Dataset

Collecting files does not create a dataset. Construction begins with the
architecture decision the data must support. The project then defines the unit
of observation, the designs and workloads that must be covered, the properties
to be measured, and the failures or unknown outcomes that must remain visible.
Those choices determine which sources are needed and which expensive tool calls
are worth acquiring.

A compact dataset-construction sequence keeps those requirements tied to the
architecture decision.

1. State the architecture decision and any transfer claim the dataset must
   support.
2. Identify the design, workload, software, and physical regions covered by
   that claim.
3. Choose sources that observe each required property under matching
   conditions.
4. Budget samples across source fidelity and acquisition cost.
5. Preserve source and candidate identity, lineage, failures, censoring,
   access, and licensing.
6. Split records by the coarsest shared ancestor relevant to the transfer
   claim.
7. Check raw returns, derived fields, and representation limits separately.
8. Record the claims that the acquired data does not support.

The first four steps shape acquisition, the next three protect identity,
lineage, and the evaluation split, and the final step records the limits of the
collection.

### Acquiring Samples Across Cost and Fidelity

Coverage needs an acquisition plan before a learned method or optimizer begins
choosing points. The plan declares the legal design regions, workloads,
conditions, and outcomes that the dataset must support. Its initial samples
should cover those groups without placing related designs or workload
derivatives on both sides of a later evaluation.

Active learning chooses the next observation whose result would be most useful
given the data already collected [@Settles2009ActiveLearning]. In architecture,
that observation is often the costly result of a simulator, formal tool,
synthesis flow, or physical-design run rather than a label supplied by a person.
Multifidelity methods perform a different job. They combine information from
sources with different costs and accuracies when those sources estimate the
same output or have an explicitly modeled relationship
[@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]. In architecture, a cheap
estimate and a costly tool result can be combined only when they address the
same property under aligned design, workload, and operating conditions, or when
their relationship has been stated and checked. Unrelated outputs do not become
multifidelity observations merely because their acquisition costs differ. The
two methods can be used together, but combining fidelities does not by itself
require adaptive selection of the next run.

Architecture projects often use *synthetic data* for four different objects
that should not share one status. A generated candidate artifact is proposed
RTL, a compiler schedule, a configuration, or a floorplan. It must pass syntax,
typing, interface, invariant, and tool-legality checks before its properties are
evaluated. A simulated observation is a return from a named simulator for a
candidate under recorded conditions, and it inherits that simulator's
abstractions and bias. A perturbed or augmented record is a derivative of a real
or simulated parent, so its lineage stays explicit and related variants remain
dependent. A predicted value substituted for an unmeasured property is an
imputation. It stays labeled as a prediction with its model, training scope,
and uncertainty, never as an observed or simulated value.

The term also describes training records sampled from a learned generator.
Such a record has a different status from the four objects above. No
architecture tool measured a property, so it is not a simulator return. An HDL
record remains proposed RTL until executable checks qualify it. A learned
sample may have no observed parent, unlike an augmentation, and it creates a
record rather than fills a missing field, unlike an imputation.
Machine-learning experiments have shown that treating learned synthetic data as
though it were real data can impair downstream generalization
[@VanBreugelEtAl2023SyntheticData]. Architecture datasets
therefore retain the generator, its training scope, the sampling procedure, and
checks against real or tool-derived observations.

These objects fail in different ways. A generator can overproduce familiar
structures and miss rare legal designs, while a simulator can report precise
values under a biased or poorly calibrated model. Perturbations preserve many
blind spots of their parents, and imputation can smooth over the constraint
boundaries that matter most. Generated artifacts therefore need legality
checks, dependent variants stay grouped by ancestor, and low-fidelity or
predicted values require property-matched calibration against sources with
stronger support for the named property.

CraftRTL illustrates a constructive use of synthetic training data. It creates
Verilog examples for non-textual specifications such as Karnaugh maps, state
transitions, and waveforms, and it builds targeted repair data from errors made
by model checkpoints [@LiuEtAl2024CraftRTL]. The reported gains apply to the
evaluated Verilog coding benchmarks. They do not make a generated module
functionally correct, connect it to a workload, or establish synthesis,
timing, power, or physical-design quality for a new project. The construction
method improves the training signal, while executable checks still determine
what a candidate supports.

A useful acquisition pattern applies cheap analytical checks to generated
candidates across a broad legal region, then spends costly observations near a
constraint boundary or decision crossover. The cheap stage prioritizes
measurements but does not enlarge support. Any claim stays inside the design,
workload, software, and physical regions where the relationship was calibrated,
together with explicit interpolation assumptions. Unobserved regions remain
unsupported.

When a selector chooses runs adaptively, the resulting dataset describes the
region that selection policy visited. Without a separate sampling
argument, it does not represent the legal design space uniformly. This book therefore
recommends retaining the selection rule, its version, the available candidate
set, and the observations available when each run was chosen. Observations
selected by the method act as policy-conditioned evidence, updating the
method under that declared policy. The reusable-holdout result provides a
precedent for protecting evaluation data when analysis adapts to earlier
answers [@DworkEtAl2015ReusableHoldout]. Architecture adds a structural
requirement to that separation. The protected boundary should follow the
transfer claim, such as a design family, workload, software revision, or later
time period, rather than consist only of randomly selected rows. Claims beyond
policy-conditioned observations require separately held-out groups or a stated
correction whose assumptions are justified for the acquisition policy.

The acquisition process must retain attempted points, failures, and censored
returns, and it must reserve design or workload groups that the selector cannot
consume. These requirements let a later reviewer distinguish broad support
from dense sampling near a predicted optimum. Method selection belongs to
@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization. The present chapter records
how that choice shaped the dataset.

### Checking Identities, Labels, and Dataset Structure

For a tool-derived dataset, one row should identify a design, software image,
workload, tool and model version, conditions, and execution attempt before it
stores a metric. Specifications, RTL or compiler graphs, traces, and tool
reports can then be aligned through those identities. Cleaning checks units,
schemas, version consistency, duplicate lineage, stale artifacts, and whether
the recorded result came from the candidate named by the row. A normalized
number with the wrong parent design is still bad data.

Machine-learning research on label errors treats the supplied label as a data
quality problem rather than hiding it inside model uncertainty
[@NorthcuttJiangChuang2021ConfidentLearning]. Research on data cascades shows
how upstream data problems can compound into delayed downstream failures
[@SambasivanEtAl2021DataCascades]. For architecture data, the corresponding
provenance chain runs from the native artifact or tool return, through the
parsed measurement and any derived field or label, to an architecture
interpretation. Each link has a different failure mode. Source corruption
damages or truncates the native return. Parser or unit errors change its value.
Stale or mismatched identities attach a valid return to the wrong design,
software, workload, or tool conditions. An incorrect derivation can assign the
wrong pass, fail, feasibility, or property label even when the parsed value is
right. Label quality therefore includes the named design, workload, tool
conditions, and property, not only the final category. Every computed field
retains the raw return and the derivation that produced it so another architect
can locate the broken link.

Outcome categories must survive those checks. An invalid request, dependency
failure, infrastructure failure, incomplete run, measured limit violation,
formal result, and unknown outcome answer different questions. Collapsing them
into a binary success label teaches a later method that a broken license server
and a physically infeasible candidate mean the same thing.

Public benchmarks add another checking problem. Models trained on public HDL
corpora may have seen the standard benchmark solutions, and contamination
studies have found this pattern in common Verilog benchmarks
[@WangEtAl2025VeriContaminated]. The same concern appears in broader
language-model evaluation [@Balloccu2024Leakage]. A benchmark score cannot
establish general design ability when the evaluated artifacts may have appeared
in training. Held-out designs, source identity, and executable checks matter
more than the volume of examples.

Held-out designs remain outside study-specific training, tuning, and method
selection until evaluation. With an opaque pretraining corpus, this separation
reduces leakage from the current study but cannot prove that a model never
encountered the design. Randomly splitting rows is also weak when nearby rows
share a repository, generator, workload trace, or time period. A useful split
must expose the transfer the project cares about, such as a new design family,
workload, or later project revision [@KapoorNarayanan2023Leakage]. Group at the
coarsest relevant shared ancestor whose separation would leak information about
the claimed transfer. For example, keep a generator family together rather than
splitting its generated variants, and keep a trace capture together rather than
splitting sampled intervals across training, tuning, and evaluation.

### Applying the Construction Sequence

OpenRTLSet provides an executed example of this sequence. The authors first
collected public Verilog, VHDL, and C/C++ repositories under licenses they
treated as permitting academic and commercial use. They screened the C/C++
sources for constructs their flow treated as unsuitable for synthesis, then ran
vhd2vl on VHDL and Vitis HLS on the screened C/C++ sources. Failed conversions
were excluded. In the C/C++ path, approximately 103,000 repositories became
approximately 12,000 after screening, and approximately 1,000 successfully
produced about 24,000 Verilog modules [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet].

The authors decomposed multi-module files so that one Verilog module became the
dataset unit. Released rows preserve the source repository URL and original
license name, pair the module with a generated description, and support model
fine-tuning followed by evaluation on VerilogEval
[@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. The source does not report a repository-disjoint
split or a released corpus of failed conversions, and the resulting row does
not certify functional correctness or preserve the full state of its source
project. This example therefore supports a scoped claim. It shows how a
licensed public-code collection became a module-level Verilog training corpus
through filtering, tool execution, cleaning, and labeling. It does not measure
the general synthesizability of public code or the coverage of industrial
architecture projects.

CircuitNet makes the missing failures visible from another direction. Its
authors attempted 12,960 back-end runs and retained 10,242 layouts after
excluding failed runs [@ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet]. The reported exclusion does
not prove that a learned model will be biased. It does make survivor-only
coverage a reasonable concern, which is an inference from the retention policy
rather than a result measured in the CircuitNet paper.

The prospective Lighthouse cache comparison shows how the same sequence would
be specified before collection. Its unit of observation is one 2, 3, or 4\ MiB
capacity candidate tied to the declared design revision, software image, XR
workload snapshot, simulator, power and SRAM models, and process assumptions.
The budget permits one SRAM evaluation per capacity and four cycle-level
executions including infrastructure reruns, with a separate status for every
attempt. A transfer claim would require a held-out design, workload, or later
time period; without those groups, the data can support only the within-study
capacity comparison. No source package or tool return has been retained, so
source access and licensing remain unresolved, and missing thermal, IR-drop,
and workload-population evidence remains visible. The complete represented
problem in @tbl-represented-problem retains the legal changes, optional learned
view, blind spots, and method handoff.

### Retaining Failed and Censored Observations

Successful designs can present a biased view of the space. When a project
retains the winning configuration while deleting failed synthesis runs,
unroutable netlists, and rejected alternatives, the remaining data cannot be
assumed to be an unbiased sample [@Rubin1976InferenceMissingData]. Retention
depends on outcome because failure itself affects whether a record survives.
Architecture adds a separate boundary argument. A negative-slack run or failed
route may be the only observation showing that a candidate crossed the feasible
region, while a crashed run may return no metric at all. Discarding those
records removes information needed to locate the boundary and can make the
feasible region look larger than the retained evidence supports.[^fn-censored-c04]

[^fn-censored-c04]: **Censored observation**: The result establishes only that a
value lies above or below a threshold rather than reporting the value itself
[@KleinMoeschberger2003Survival]. A target-frequency test that reports only a
failure is left-censored because it establishes that the maximum sustainable
frequency lies below the target.

An execution history must separate three fields that are easy to blur. Attempt
status records whether a tool invocation completed, failed, timed out, or was
retried. Candidate outcome records whether the resulting evidence supports
advancing the candidate, rejecting it, or leaving the comparison unresolved.
Project update records whether an authorized decision changed the accepted
design state. Keeping these fields separate prevents dataset cleaning from
turning a tool failure into design evidence or a completed measurement into a
state change (@fig-execution-history). The lifecycle mechanics for advancing
work and changing accepted project state remain in
@sec-architecture-20-ontology.

![**Execution history preserves three separate fields:** Attempt
status records actual tool completion or failure, candidate outcome records
what the result supports for the current comparison, and project update records
whether accepted design state changed. Stale inputs can yield a completed
attempt with no usable candidate outcome and no project
update.](images/F4-trajectory-record){#fig-execution-history width="85%"
fig-alt="Versioned execution history with separate attempt status, candidate
outcome, and project update fields. One completed attempt advances a candidate
and creates a new project version. A second completed attempt leaves the
candidate rejected or unresolved and makes no project update. A third attempt
completes on stale inputs, which yields no usable candidate outcome for the
current comparison and leaves project state unchanged."}

The branches in @fig-execution-history illustrate schema values rather than
live Lighthouse outcomes. A prior result becomes a comparable sample only when
its design, candidate, workload, software, tool, and physical-condition
identities satisfy the matching rule in @tbl-represented-problem. Other records
can remain visible as advisory context without becoming samples for this study.

Projects need negative records because successful designs are survivor
samples. The record should preserve why a run failed without turning one local
result into a universal prohibition (@tbl-negative-traces).

| **Failed run or rejected alternative** | **What to keep** | **How later work should use it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Synthesis or timing violation** | Candidate, constraints, process assumptions, and failing paths. | Reconsider the candidate only after checking whether the relevant conditions still apply. |
| **Unroutable or power-delivery failure** | Netlist, placement conditions, density, congestion, or IR-drop result. | Identify the affected region and avoid treating the failure as a property of all similar designs. |
| **Proxy improvement overturned later** | Cheap estimate, later observation, and the conditions under which they diverged. | Reassess the proxy's useful scope before reuse. |
| **Tool failure or crash** | Command, inputs, environment identity, logs, and failure classification. | Repair the environment without recording the candidate as architecturally rejected. |
| **Coverage gap** | Missing workload, input, scenario, or architecture class. | Mark the boundary of the result rather than filling it with an assumption. |
| **Reviewer rejection** | Candidate, stated reason, risk, schedule, integration concern, and decision owner. | Preserve the rationale and revisit it only when the relevant conditions change. |
| **Waiver or exception** | Violated rule, justification, scope, owner, and expiration or review condition. | Prevent repeated work while keeping the exception visible. |

: **Rejected work remains useful when its conditions are recorded.** A later
architect can determine whether the same boundary still applies.
{#tbl-negative-traces tbl-colwidths="[27,34,29]"}

Later reuse depends on the kind of failure. Timing, routing, or power-delivery
failures may constrain a candidate when the same design and conditions recur. A
tool crash instead returns to environment repair and must not become a
candidate rejection. Waivers similarly retain their scope, owner, and review
condition rather than turning an exception into a general pass.

The finished dataset records provenance, versions, access and licensing
conditions, acquisition cost, omitted populations, leakage risks, and the
reason each missing value is absent. These checks do not prove that the dataset
will support every later use. They make its support and omissions visible
enough for another architect to decide whether it applies. A checked dataset
still records what sources returned, not which project facts apply now. Current
facts must come from the authoritative project sources that own them.

## From Data to Architecture Knowledge and Current State

Recorded data, durable knowledge, and live state answer different questions.
Data consists of source artifacts, measurements, check results, and decisions
captured under stated conditions. Durable project knowledge includes
specifications, recurring design rationale, prior measurements, and resolved
decisions that may remain useful across tasks. Live project state names the
hardware, software, workload, constraints, unresolved issues, and accepted
revisions that apply now.

A method may need all three, but they change at different rates and come from
different responsible sources. A paper can explain why cache capacity may
affect misses, but it cannot override the checked-in design. A retrieved manual
can clarify a tool option, but it cannot establish which option the current run
used. An old run can reveal a risk, but it cannot automatically stand in for a
current measurement.

An architecture foundation model contributes broad prior knowledge learned
across sources. It can help retrieve a relevant mechanism, classify a familiar
interface pattern, or suggest which project document to inspect. It cannot
supply the current design revision, software image, workload, constraint, open
issue, or accepted tool result unless those facts arrive through current,
source-linked project context.

No single object owns every project fact. Each preserves a different kind of
knowledge or state, with its own responsible source and freshness rule.
Collapsing these objects into a generic term like *memory* or *context* obscures when one object may
inform a decision and when another remains authoritative
(@tbl-knowledge-objects).

| **Object** | **What it preserves** | **Responsible source and freshness rule** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Trained-model weights** | Learned statistical regularities and general concepts. | Useful as prior knowledge, never the source of record for current project state. |
| **Retrieval index and retrieved material** | Source-linked manuals, papers, examples, and project documents selected for the current task. | The underlying source remains responsible. Version and date must match the use. |
| **In-context working set** | Instructions, selected sources, current state, and examples needed for one operation. | Transient assembly only. It does not become project state until a recorded update changes the responsible source. |
| **Defined comparison** | Question, comparator, scope, permitted changes, constraints, measurements, budget, and stopping conditions. | Remains the authoritative comparison definition until its owner records a revision. |
| **Current design and software artifacts** | Configuration, generated hardware, software image, manifests, and linked constraints. | Current only when the authoritative sources agree and consistency checks pass. |
| **Workload state** | Trace, profile, population, phase definitions, sampling policy, and version. | Controls the workload condition only within its recorded coverage. |
| **Project history** | Prior candidates, tool runs, failures, decisions, and rationale linked to their conditions. | Records what happened then, but does not make that result applicable to the current version. |

: **Knowledge objects preserve different facts.** The current value comes from
the authoritative source for that part of the project, not from whichever
object was supplied most recently.
{#tbl-knowledge-objects tbl-colwidths="[23,38,29]"}

There is no safe global rule that one file always wins. The defined comparison
states the permitted differences. The checked-in configuration and generated
artifact define implemented hardware state when they agree. The workload
manifest identifies the current trace. The specification states an interface
requirement. A review decision records whether a candidate advanced. Each fact
comes from its authoritative source. When those sources disagree, the project
does not silently favor the most convenient one. Work stops until the owner
reconciles the mismatch or records a revision.

These objects change on different schedules. Model training may capture general
relationships, while retrieval supplies manuals and prior reports when they are
needed. Current constraints belong in explicit project state, not in model
weights. Tool results enter project history only after their identity and
conditions are known. Fast-changing facts need an explicit, versioned path.
Slow-changing knowledge can inform the work, but it cannot override those
facts.

The current working context assembles the subset needed for one operation, but
only a versioned change to an authoritative source can revise the comparison,
design, workload, constraint, or accepted result. That change records its owner,
dependencies, and consistency checks. Fresh context alone cannot turn advisory
knowledge into current project state.

Freshness is part of the distinction between durable knowledge and live state.
A current retrieval index can point to an old manual. A current design can be
paired with a trace captured from an earlier software image. A run directory
can contain a new report and an old configuration. Each file may look plausible
in isolation, but the combination might describe a design that never existed
(@fig-split-brain-causality).

![**A stale source can make a current design appear internally
consistent.** When a method reads an earlier specification or project state, it
can propose a change that violates the version now under
design.](images/F4b-split-brain-causality){#fig-split-brain-causality
width="100%" fig-alt="A stale reference state and a current project state lead
to an incompatible proposal. Version and freshness checks expose the mismatch
before the proposal reaches a costly tool flow."}

A proposal derived from reference V1 can appear internally consistent while
violating the design under development at V2. The version mismatch should stop
that proposal before it reaches an expensive tool path.

The represented state can also drift from the artifact it claims to describe.
A parameter is renamed in the generator, a constraint is tightened directly in
an SDC file, or a block is replaced by hand. The state still says it is current,
but regenerating the design produces something different from the checked-in
artifact.

The direct check is to regenerate the artifact from the represented state and
compare the result with the repository. If the state cannot reproduce the
design it names, work that depends on it should not start. This check has a
clear limit: it works only where the state owns generation. A hand edit below
that level must be detected by another consistency check or made an explicit
part of state.

Source identity needs enough detail to support these checks. Depending on the
artifact, that may mean a version-control revision, content hash, tool and model
version, workload manifest, seed, process corner, timestamp, or named owner. The
representation should keep only what the study needs, but it cannot omit the
identity required to decide whether two records describe the same conditions.

Current state also has a maintenance cost. A freshness check reports a
condition at one moment. It does not keep the state current. Each source that
could change the decision needs a named owner and an invalidation trigger. A
new design revision, compiler release, workload capture, tool calibration,
constraint, library, process assumption, or expired waiver can make some part
of the represented problem stale.

When a trigger occurs, the owner determines which dependent artifacts and
results are affected. The response may be to regenerate an artifact, rerun a
consistency check, recapture data, recalibrate a model, repeat a measurement, or
mark the earlier result unavailable for the current comparison. The dependency
links matter because they keep a compiler update from forcing unrelated
physical work while ensuring that a changed cache generator reaches the
configurations, RTL, constraints, tests, and results that depend on it.

This maintenance consumes the same resources that data acquisition does.
Regeneration and checking use compute, licenses, storage, and tool time.
Recapturing a workload or recalibrating a model uses data and engineering time.
Broken links and source conflicts require diagnosis and review. Those recurring
costs should remain separate in the project record so that maintaining a rich
representation is not treated as free and so a later evaluation can see
whether the retained state repaid its cost.

Not every source should be maintained forever. When refresh cost exceeds the
value of keeping a source live, the project can narrow the representation,
freeze a versioned snapshot with an explicit review condition, or retain the
missing relationship as a blind spot. A source with no owner, invalidation
trigger, or affordable refresh path is historical context, not current project
state.

Correctly separated data, knowledge, and live state still cannot guide a
method unless the needed properties are exposed in a usable form. The native
artifact may remain authoritative while a derived encoding hides the
relationship that the task needs.

## From Architecture Artifacts to Learned Representations

A project can have the right facts and still represent them badly. The encoding
decides which designs can be expressed, which dependencies remain connected,
and which changes a later method will regard as nearby.

Raw text is useful for explanation but weak as the sole representation of a
design. It can describe an L2 change without identifying the configuration
field, affected interfaces, or companion constraints. Tool-facing
representations add structure. Parameter schemas enumerate legal values.
Abstract syntax trees and data-flow graphs preserve relationships that a token
sequence makes difficult to inspect. Typed intermediate representations can
reject malformed constructions before expensive execution. Parameterized
generators can expose a bounded set of changes while retaining the lowering
path to RTL.

Typed representations are not safe in general. They reject only violations
covered by their types and checks. SystemVerilog specifies logic, hierarchy,
interfaces, and verification constructs [@IEEE2023SystemVerilog]. FIRRTL and
typed dialects in Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT) expose operations,
types, and compiler transformations [@CIRCT; @Izraelevitz2017Chisel]. Companion formats such as
Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) and Unified Power Format (UPF) carry timing
and power intent [@SynopsysSDC; @IEEE2024UPF]. Each preserves different
properties (@tbl-representation-formats).

| **Representation** | **What it makes explicit** | **What still requires attention** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SystemVerilog or VHDL | Logic, hierarchy, interfaces, and behavior in the HDL. | Width conventions, connectivity, unknown values, verification intent, and all properties not established by compilation. |
| Typed hardware IR such as FIRRTL or a CIRCT dialect | Operations, types, connectivity, and transformations supported by the IR. | Legal designs the IR cannot express, semantic correctness, lowering, verification, and physical realization. |
| Parameter schema and generator | Named mutable fields, legal values, and a reproducible path to generated artifacts. | Whether the generator and checked-in artifacts agree and whether dependent collateral changes with the design. |
| SDC, UPF, and other constraint collateral | Timing, power intent, domains, path references, and implementation assumptions. | Hierarchical-name coupling, stale paths, waived checks, and consistency with the RTL. |
| Graph or spatial representation | Connectivity, topology, adjacency, or physical location. | Features omitted from nodes and edges, write-back to tool inputs, and physical rules not encoded in the graph. |
| Learned embedding or latent feature vector | Statistical similarity and directions learned from the data supplied during training or adaptation. | Exact artifact identity, hierarchy, topology, order, units, legality, constraints, uncertainty, source coverage, and check results. |

: **A representation makes some properties explicit and leaves others for
later checks.** Choosing one also chooses which legal designs are easy,
difficult, or impossible to express.
{#tbl-representation-formats tbl-colwidths="[24,34,32]"}

An embedding is a learned vector representation whose similarities or
directions can be useful to downstream learning tasks
[@BengioEtAl2013RepresentationLearning]. It is one learned representation
among several, not a compressed replacement for the source artifact. The
project must retain a link back to the exact source and to the properties that
cannot safely be recovered from learned similarity.

A learned representation also needs a task-specific fitness test. The project
states the learning objective and training data, names changes that should
leave the representation invariant, and names distinctions that must remain
visible. It then probes neighbors and counterexamples on held-out design
groups. If a representation drives artifact generation or mutation, proposed
changes must round-trip to the native representation and pass the applicable
legality and tool checks. An embedding that supports retrieval can still be
unfit for prediction or design modification when its geometry collapses a
topological, timing, or physical distinction needed by the later task.

Native sources can therefore feed several derived forms without surrendering
their original meaning. The useful question is which capability a derived form
enables and which exact information must remain linked outside it
(@tbl-source-representation-capability).

| **Native source** | **Structured or learned representation** | **Capability it can support** | **Exact information that stays linked** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Specification, manual, or design document | Versioned text chunks, typed requirement records, retrieval index, or text embedding. | Retrieve requirements, rationale, interface descriptions, and prior decisions. | Source identity, revision, access status, exact requirement text, and responsible owner. |
| Source code, RTL, netlist, or compiler IR | Token sequence, abstract syntax tree, typed IR, connectivity graph, or learned graph representation. | Inspect structure, propose bounded edits, retrieve similar blocks, or estimate a named property. | Native artifact, hierarchy, types, topology, legal transformations, companion constraints, and tool-check results. |
| Trace, performance counter stream, or profile | Phase record, sequence, time series, aggregate feature vector, or learned workload embedding. | Characterize phases, retrieve similar behavior, select samples, or predict a scoped response. | Input, software version, event order, timestamps, scale, sampling policy, units, and coverage. |
| Floorplan, physical database, or tool report | Geometry, spatial graph, typed report fields, image-like tensor, or learned physical representation. | Retrieve related layouts, localize physical pressure, or estimate a declared implementation property. | Coordinate system, units, design and tool version, mode, corner, constraints, waivers, uncertainty, raw artifact, and returned check status. |

: **Derived representations add capabilities only while exact architecture
facts stay connected to their sources.** Text, graphs, sequences, spatial
forms, and embeddings expose different properties, so the project retains the
native artifact and the conditions that make each derived view meaningful.
{#tbl-source-representation-capability tbl-colwidths="[20,28,24,28]"}

For a physical design, a graph, tensor, embedding, or image-like view is not
itself an authoritative database edit. A proposed change must write back
through the authoritative database or a reproducible tool command, then repeat
legalization and the implementation checks that the change can affect.

Each row connects a native source to a structured or learned form and the
capability that form can support. The final column is not another
learned-feature list. It protects source identity, hierarchy, topology, order,
units, legality, exact constraints, uncertainty, and returned check results in
forms that another tool or architect can inspect.

::: {.callout-field-note title="The missing level shifter"}
**The expectation.** A text-based proposal that connects logic across two
voltage domains and passes syntax checks represents a legal crossing, including
any required level shifter.

**In practice.** The proposal omits the level shifter because the represented
design lacks the power-domain relationship that makes the connection illegal.

**The lesson.** Better prose would not fix the problem. The design state must
carry the domains and the required crossing rule in a form the tool path can
check. If the omission survives into downstream implementation, the team must
regenerate affected
collateral, repeat regressions, reopen timing closure, and rerun physical
verification. If the illegal crossing escapes into silicon, recovery may
require a respin rather than a cheap rollback. The missing relationship
therefore changes both the correctness risk and the cost of discovering the
error.
:::

Hardware is concurrent and relational. A netlist is a graph, a memory hierarchy
is a topology, and a floorplan adds spatial coordinates. Graph encodings can
preserve fan-in, fan-out, connectivity, and structural locality more directly
than a one-dimensional token stream. DeepGate2, for example, learns over
and-inverter graphs rather than treating a circuit only as text
[@ShiEtAl2023DeepGate2]. A graph still omits any property not attached to its
nodes, edges, or surrounding state. Logical adjacency is not physical
proximity, and a graph without placement cannot establish wire delay.

Mirhoseini and colleagues' macro-placement work provides a useful
representation example. The chip was represented with graph structure for
connectivity and a grid-like canvas for legal placement. Those choices exposed
relationships and spatial actions that flat RTL text did not
[@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement]. The result
does not establish that one placement method is generally best. It shows that a
method can search only after the architecture problem has been translated into
a form that preserves the relationships relevant to the task. The graph and
canvas also remain derived views of the native placement state rather than
independent sources of truth. A usable architecture representation keeps those
links intact. The placement method and its objective belong with optimization
in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization rather than in this chapter.

## Choosing and Connecting Representations

No single representation should carry every architecture responsibility. The
native artifact preserves exact content and remains the object that tools build
or check. Explicit structures expose hierarchy, topology, order, units,
constraints, and legal transformations. Retrieved context supplies
source-linked requirements and rationale. Learned representations can support
similarity, retrieval, prediction, generation, or adaptation, but they do not
replace those exact forms.

The representations must remain connected. A workload embedding without its
software and sampling record, a graph without its source hierarchy, or a report
vector without its units and tool conditions cannot be traced back to the fact
it is supposed to represent. The choice is therefore not one universal format,
but rather a set of linked views chosen for the downstream capability and checked
against the properties each view must preserve.

The default is deliberately conservative. Retain the authoritative native
artifact, add the minimum explicit structure needed to expose legal actions,
constraints, and dependencies, and add a learned representation only when it
enables a named capability that justifies its validation and maintenance cost.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Choose representations by what the decision must preserve"}
Select representations based strictly on the properties a downstream decision must preserve, not merely for convenience or statistical model fit. If a selected view drops critical architectural invariants (such as object identity, legality, topology, temporal order, physical units, or cross-layer links), an automated method will generate plausible but illegal designs. Ensure every decision-critical property is traceable to an inspectable, authoritative form. You may abstract away irrelevant detail only if the loss is explicit and the resulting structural claims are strictly qualified.
:::

### Permitted Changes and Invariants

A representation must separate what may change from what must remain fixed. In
the prospective Lighthouse cache study, L2 capacity is the only mutable
architecture field. The 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB choices must map to
realizable cache configurations.
Cache policy, NoC topology, compiler, runtime, software image, workload, and the
rest of the memory system remain fixed. The 3\ W power envelope, 1.5\ mm^2^
macro-area limit, 2.5\ ns access-time allocation, and independent thermal and
IR-drop review remain required.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="One permitted change, with its dependencies"}
**Declared context and change.** Compare realizable 2, 3, and 4\ MiB L2
capacities for the same XR workload and system state.

**What assistance may change.** A method may select the capacity and update the
generated cache instance and dependent configuration needed to realize it.

**Required invariants and checks.** Cache policy, NoC topology, compiler,
runtime, software image, workload snapshot, and memory system remain fixed.
Every candidate still faces the declared power, area, access-time, thermal, and
IR-drop checks.
