**Takeaway and reformulation boundary.** A proposal that also changes compiler
behavior may be worth studying, but it answers a different architecture
question and requires a reformulated comparison.
:::

The distinction also separates parametric and structural changes. A parametric
change selects a value within an existing structure, such as a legal cache
capacity or queue depth. A structural change alters the set of components or
relationships, such as adding a pipeline stage, replacing a mesh with a ring,
or inserting an accelerator. Structural changes require a different schema,
different dependent artifacts, and often a different study. Calling both
changes simply *edits* hides the difference.

System and software contracts matter even when they live outside the local
configuration. A new vector instruction affects the ISA, compiler, runtime,
and verification plan, and it may also require control and status register
changes. A memory organization that
improves average latency but violates the memory consistency model is not a
legal system design. Backward compatibility, interface standards, and
software assumptions must appear as dependencies or invariants rather than
remaining with the one experienced engineer who remembers them.

Physical collateral is coupled in the same way. Timing constraints often refer
to exact hierarchical paths. Renaming or moving a block without updating or
remapping its SDC can leave a constraint attached to the wrong design object or
to nothing [@Synopsys2023ConstraintMapping]. Power intent is separate companion
state that must remain aligned with the matching RTL hierarchy
[@IEEE2024UPF]. A legal change therefore includes its required companion
changes. The representation should make that group visible so a later method
cannot improve one file while silently invalidating another.

Fixed conditions may also be a set rather than one point. Multi-corner,
multi-mode analysis represents a physical design across operating modes and
timing-analysis views defined by their operating conditions and libraries
[@Cadence2021Tempus].
A candidate must retain the same identity across the declared condition matrix,
and each result must name the condition it covers. A typical-corner result
cannot silently stand in for a fast-corner hold check or a low-power operating
mode.

### Encoding Changes the Geometry

Even a correct list of legal values imposes a geometry on later search. Suppose
cache capacity is encoded on a linear numerical axis. A move from 512\ KiB to
1\ MiB then appears to be the same distance as a move from 4\ MiB to 4.5\ MiB.
The architectural effects are unlikely to be comparable, and 4.5\ MiB may not
be realizable with the available SRAM macros. The encoding has created a
misleading neighborhood and an impossible point.

Two checks expose the problem. First, compare adjacent steps at different parts
of the encoded range. If equal encoded steps produce very different changes in
the architectural quantity of interest, the distance is misleading. Second,
ask whether every encoded point lowers to a configuration the tools can build.
An index over realizable macro organizations may be better than a continuous
capacity value. A logarithmic capacity axis may better reflect some cache
relationships than a linear one. These are design inferences for this example,
not prescriptions from one modeling paper. More broadly, classical
architecture design-space models use transformations and nonlinear terms when
parameter effects and interactions are not well represented on the original
axes [@LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling].

The lesson does not prescribe an optimizer. It precedes method selection.
Generation, prediction, and optimization all inherit the reachable set and
neighborhood created here. A poor encoding can make any of them waste effort
on impossible candidates or miss useful ones that were never expressible.
Every legal searchable action must also remain linked to the downstream
artifacts and checks it changes.

### Cross-Layer Relationships Need Provenance

Freshness also runs vertically through the stack. A high-level decision such as
adding a prefetcher may be lowered through generators, RTL, synthesis,
placement, and timing analysis. If a later timing failure cannot be connected
back to the architecture construct that produced it, the design state
fragments when the team most needs an explanation.

Cross-layer provenance records those relationships. It connects architecture
intent to the implementation objects and constraints that realize it. It does
not prove that every transformation preserved meaning. It makes the chain
inspectable and can localize a missing link or failed consistency check.
Detecting semantic loss still requires a check for the property that should
have survived.

Common architecture artifacts become reusable only when their hidden context is
made visible (@tbl-representation-debt).

| **Artifact** | **What it preserves** | **What it often hides** | **Resulting blind spot** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Paper or plot | Reported claim, result, and comparison. | Tool flags, failed candidates, and tuning history. | The endpoint is visible but the path cannot be reconstructed. |
| Workload trace | Captured input behavior and measurements. | Population, coverage, version, sampling, and privacy filters. | The design may be optimized for an unrepresentative slice. |
| Simulator configuration | Model settings and selected options. | Defaults, unsupported states, calibration limits, and dependent software. | A number may be trusted outside the simulator's useful scope. |
| RTL or EDA report | Implementation-facing structure or feedback. | Process assumptions, constraints, waived warnings, and intent. | A locally valid artifact may not satisfy the system decision. |
| Cross-layer mapping | Links from architecture choices to lower-level objects. | Intermediate transformations not recorded in the mapping. | A physical failure may not be traceable to the choice that caused it. |
| Review note | Judgment, rationale, risk, and decision. | Unstated assumptions or alternatives never entered into the record. | Later work remembers the verdict but not its conditions. |
| Rejected candidate | A boundary and a negative result. | Failure reason, tool path, workload, or design version. | The team either repeats the failure or excludes too much. |

: **Architecture artifacts are reusable only within their recorded context.**
Provenance, assumptions, constraints, and coverage expose what each artifact
does and does not support.
{#tbl-representation-debt tbl-colwidths="[20,28,27,25]"}

Hidden context determines whether an artifact can be reused. A paper, plot, or
review note may preserve an endpoint or verdict without the path and conditions
that produced it. An RTL or EDA report may be locally valid without supporting
the system decision, while a cross-layer mapping can still hide an intermediate
transformation. Reuse therefore depends on preserving the context that rules
out each blind spot, not on the artifact type alone.

### Blind Spots and Known Unknowns Stay Visible

An adequate representation is not one that contains everything. It states what
it contains, what it omits, and the scope within which it remains useful.
Building a complete digital description of a modern system would cost more than
most studies could justify and would still miss something.

Blind spots are omitted or unobserved relationships that could matter. The
prospective Lighthouse cache representation has no detailed floorplan or
congestion result, no completed thermal or IR-drop review, and no guarantee that
the declared XR workload snapshot covers every deployed workload condition.
Known unknowns are questions already recognized but not yet resolved, such as
whether a larger cache improves tail frame time enough to advance.

A known unknown can be planned for, whereas a blind spot may surface only after
a later tool, reviewer, or field observation exposes it.
Both should remain visible so that a later method does not convert missing
information into an assumed favorable value.

The prospective Lighthouse cache comparison tests whether these source, state,
and blind-spot distinctions can be made concrete in one problem description.

### Applying the Representation to the Lighthouse Cache Study

The Lighthouse application is a compact handoff rather than a second account
of the chapter. It binds the cache question to the exact design and workload
state, legal change, constraints, observations, and missing checks needed to
interpret a later result. @tbl-represented-problem gives the minimum useful
description for that comparison. A longer-lived or more consequential use
needs more retained history and source identity. The rules for claims that
leave the project belong to the later discussion of decision responsibility.

Completeness is not the test for the description. A later reader has to be able
to interpret a result from it without asking the original team what was
assumed.

| **Part of the problem** | **Representation for the prospective Lighthouse cache study** |
| --- | --- |
| **Architecture question and permitted change** | At the current design revision, determine which, if either, of the 3\ MiB and 4\ MiB settings should advance against a rerun 2\ MiB baseline. Only `l2.capacity` may change, and each value must resolve to one realizable cache configuration. |
| **Fixed hardware, software, and workload state** | Cache policy, associativity, NoC topology, memory system, the 2\ GHz microarchitecture, compiler, runtime, and RISC-V software image remain fixed. The versioned XR workload snapshot must retain stable frame identifiers and boundaries, collection policy, coverage, and owner. The generator revision, generated cache instance, and linked implementation collateral must remain aligned with the selected capacity. |
| **Exact source and version identities** | Each record carries a comparison key covering the study revision, design revision, candidate configuration, workload snapshot, software image, tool-chain manifest, and physical-condition set. Every field resolves to an exact source, version or hash, and owner. Derived configurations, cache instances, measurements, and later decisions retain lineage to that key. These remain specification identities because this prospective example has no retained source package or execution artifact. |
| **Constraints and checks** | Each candidate must identify versioned reference behavior, testbench or properties, coverage intent, interface and reset assumptions, and required checks. Modeled subsystem dynamic plus leakage power must not exceed 3\ W, cache macro area 1.5\ mm^2^, or modeled access time 2.5\ ns. Thermal and IR-drop reviews remain independent later checks. |
| **Observations, history, and acquisition cost** | The execution history is initially empty. The budget permits four cycle-level executions including infrastructure reruns and one SRAM evaluation per capacity. Each attempt retains status, cost, raw returns, and derived fields. A prior result becomes a comparable sample only when the relevant comparison-key fields match; other results remain advisory context. |
| **Cross-layer relationships** | Capacity can change miss behavior and the frame-time distribution. It also changes macro organization and may affect power, area, access time, and physical integration. Candidate results must remain linked to the workload, software, cache policy, memory system, generated artifact, constraints, and checks that give those effects meaning. |
| **Optional learned view** | For retrieval or prediction, a learned embedding or feature vector could combine workload-phase behavior with cache and memory-system features. A retriever could locate similar prior cases, or a predictor estimate 99th-percentile frame time. The learned view remains linked to the exact workload snapshot, software image, candidate, tool-chain version, physical-condition set, and target definition. It cannot carry exact legality, units, or hard power, area, and access-time limits by itself; the authoritative schema and checks retain them. |
| **Blind spots and known unknowns** | The representation contains no retained floorplan, congestion result, workload snapshot, completed thermal or IR-drop review, or evidence that the declared workload covers every deployed condition. It may miss effects outside the named tools. Open questions include whether either larger cache improves 99th-percentile frame time enough to advance and whether later physical review exposes an omitted effect. |
| **Useful scope and handoff** | The representation supports this cache-capacity comparison and selection of at most one candidate for later RTL evaluation. It excludes changes to cache policy, prefetching, coherence, NoC, compiler, software scheduling, floorplanning, thermal or IR-drop signoff, security, reliability, and product cost. It passes @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization an inspectable problem, not a complete model of the XR subsystem or a selected method. |

: **The represented problem makes the cache comparison inspectable.** It
connects exact design and workload identities, legal changes, checks, history,
freshness, and limits without selecting a method or claiming a result.
{#tbl-represented-problem tbl-colwidths="[24,66]"}

The first four groups establish the comparison and its checks. The next two
retain what was observed and connect each observation to the architecture
relationships that produced it. The optional learned view can add retrieval or
prediction without replacing exact state. The final two expose unsupported
inferences and bound the handoff. The decisive link maps `l2.capacity` to one
realizable cache configuration while the workload, software, cache policy,
memory system, and constraints remain tied to every comparison.

In a future execution, the fields may live in several project systems. What
matters is that every retained artifact refers to the same study, design
version, workload version, and candidate. A directory full of individually
valid files is not a represented problem if no one can tell which files
describe the same comparison.

### Inputs to Method Choice

Method choice can begin only when the represented problem is sufficient to
judge method fit. For the prospective Lighthouse cache comparison,
@tbl-represented-problem supplies the intended design revision, legal changes,
sample conditions and acquisition cost, expected status distinctions,
connected native and learned representations, blind spots, freshness rules,
and useful scope. It intentionally supplies no proposed candidate,
prediction, surrogate, optimizer, acceptance threshold for a model, or
execution result. The handoff to method choice is a represented problem, not a
prescribed technique.

The handoff is inadequate if it cannot reproduce or identify the current
design, if it hides a controlling hardware-software or physical relationship,
if its legal actions bundle undeclared changes, if its sources disagree without
a resolution, or if no one can state where the representation is useful.

## Common Pitfalls

When managing architecture data and building representations, it is easy to inadvertently corrupt the integrity of your models or datasets. The following mistakes frequently occur when generic data science practices are applied to complex hardware design environments without accounting for the dependencies, hard constraints, and missingness inherent in architecture workflows.

**Letting Related Artifacts Cross the Train-Test Boundary.** Splitting variants from the same repository, generator family, workload trace, or project revision across training and evaluation sets is a common error. This data leakage makes simple recognition look like successful generalization to a new design, resulting in models that fail on truly unseen architectures.

**Keeping Only Successful Runs.** Deleting failed synthesis, negative-slack, unroutable, power-limited, or timed-out runs causes a dangerous survivorship bias. It makes the feasible design space look artificially larger than it is and trains later methods to steer toward invalid or physically impossible proposals because they never learn where the boundaries lie.

**Treating a Learned View as the Design Record.** An embedding or learned feature space can preserve statistical similarity while losing exact legality, physical units, topology, order, timing, power constraints, or tool conditions. Treating this learned view as a substitute for the authoritative source of record often allows a close-looking candidate to be accepted, even if it is fundamentally illegal or physically invalid.

## Open Questions

The central open problems concern acquiring costly and incomplete architecture
data, preserving design relationships across representations, and keeping
project knowledge current.

**Building architecture datasets.** Architecture data comes from sources with
different costs, coverage, failure modes, authority, and access limits.

- **How can synthetic and low-fidelity data expand coverage without hiding
  unsupported regions?** Synthetic observations can make a dataset look broad
  while repeating the assumptions and blind spots of the model that produced
  them. The hard part is determining where low-cost data still reflects real
  workload and implementation behavior and where stronger measurements are
  required.

- **How should an architecture team retain and use failed and censored runs
  without treating local failure as a universal boundary?** A failed tool run,
  an infeasible candidate, a limit violation, and an unobserved outcome do not
  mean the same thing. Their meaning depends on the design, workload, tool path,
  and constraints that produced them, yet removing them erases information
  about where a method fails. Preserving that distinction without turning a
  local failure into a universal rule remains difficult at dataset scale.

- **How can a private architecture dataset support an independently testable
  result without exposing restricted artifacts?** Private datasets can support
  important results even when designs, traces, or tool outputs cannot be
  released. Useful disclosure must let an independent reviewer test the claim
  and its limits as release conditions range from fully private to fully public.

**Representing architecture knowledge and current state.** Learned and explicit
representations must support useful generalization while preserving exact
constraints, source identity, and freshness.

- **How can learned representations capture useful similarity without hiding
  exact architecture constraints?** A learned representation may capture
  statistical similarity while smoothing over an ISA requirement, interface
  rule, or physical limit that must remain exact. The challenge is to combine
  generalization with explicit constraints so that useful transfer does not
  make illegal or untraceable candidates appear valid.

- **How can an automated method detect that represented project state no longer
  describes the artifact it names?** Project state can diverge when hand edits,
  generated collateral, external tools, and delayed results update different
  artifacts at different times. Constantly rebuilding everything is costly, but
  stale state can invalidate later simulation or implementation work. Research
  must identify which changes require renewed checks before an automated method
  relies on the represented state.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Keep every observation tied to the conditions that produced it"}
Enforce strict provenance by linking every observation directly to the exact design, workload, software image, tool configurations, and acquisition constraints that produced it. Failing to preserve this lineage allows stale or conditionally mismatched data to corrupt downstream comparisons. Critically, you must retain timeouts and failed tool runs; dropping them artificially inflates the feasible design space. Record all conditions that affect applicability or explain an outcome, ensuring that any reviewer or automated method can independently verify whether a historical sample applies to the current design candidate.
:::

Architecture data is not a collection of interchangeable labeled examples.
Specifications, code, RTL, traces, formal results, tool reports, rejected work,
and reviews carry different information. Workloads determine which behavior is
exercised, and every stored result remains tied to the design, software, tool,
conditions, and acquisition cost that produced it. Coverage matters more than
row count.

A usable dataset makes those dependencies inspectable. It aligns source
identities and units, checks versions and lineage, preserves failures and
censored results, separates tool problems from measured design violations, and
documents held-out designs, access limits, omissions, and leakage risks. This
work turns heterogeneous sources into data that a later method can use without
making unsupported comparisons look clean.

Data does not replace project knowledge or live state. A foundation model can
supply broad prior knowledge, and retrieval can bring source-linked material
into the current task. The checked-in design, software image, workload,
constraints, unresolved issues, and accepted results still come from current
project sources. A state that cannot identify or reproduce the artifact it
names is not current.

Native artifacts, typed structures, graphs, sequences, spatial forms, retrieved
text, and learned representations each expose different properties. Embeddings
can support useful similarity and adaptation, but identity, hierarchy,
topology, order, legality, units, exact constraints, uncertainty, and returned
check results remain linked outside them. The architect chooses connected
representations that preserve the relationships controlling the current
question and expose what remains missing.

The represented problem in @tbl-represented-problem binds source identity,
workload, sample conditions and cost, checked data, current state, legal
changes, dependencies, history, linked representations, freshness, blind
spots, and known unknowns for the prospective Lighthouse cache study. Those
fields prevent method choice from inventing missing state or comparing
incompatible records. The remaining question is which approach fits that
represented problem. @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization takes up that
choice.
